newsitem.title: UK: Adams-N.Irish poll victor and conflict veteran.
newsitem.headline: Adams-N.Irish poll victor and conflict veteran.

text.p: Demonised by Britain but lionised by his supporters, Gerry Adams, head of the IRA's Sinn Fein political arm, swept to victory on Friday, recapturing the key West Belfast seat in Britain's parliamentary election.
Leader of Sinn Fein since 1983, he has now been elected three times to represent the constituency which for years has been the cockpit of a guerrilla drive against British rule.
But Adams, 48, is "an abstentionist" who refuses to sit in the London legislature. To do so, he says, would be to recognise Britain's right to rule Northern Ireland.
Britain says a wave of Irish Republican Army (IRA) bombings proves that the guerrillas and Sinn Fein are hand-in-hand in a strategy to end British rule by a combination of bomb and ballot box.

Shunned by British, Irish and U.S. leaders since an IRA truce collapsed early last year, Adams denies links between Sinn Fein and the IRA. He proclaims commitment to a "peace strategy" based on talks and an end to violence on all sides.
Tall, bearded and bespectacled, he has achieved a global political profile for republicanism unrivalled since the island was partitioned in 1922.
His rise to power has tormented the British.

Adams was a teenage bartender in downtown Belfast before becoming steeped in a hardline republicanism that aimed to destroy British rule and single-party Protestant domination and join Northern Ireland into an all-Ireland state.
A key activist during a Catholic campaign for civil rights in the late 1960s, he was interned by the British as a suspected IRA warlord when the province toppled into guerrilla war.
Released from the notorious Long Kesh internment camp in 1972, he was flown secretly to London with IRA commanders for what proved to be abortive peace talks with a British minister.
Re-arrested in 1973, he failed in a bid to escape from Long Kesh and was eventually freed from prison in 1976.
In a climate of almost-daily battles between British forces and IRA fighters, and Protestant "Loyalist" death squads marauding through Catholic zones, Adams emerged as a major political strategist.
He told supporters they could not win their goal of a United Ireland by military means alone. He set about injecting new life into an almost moribund Sinn Fein.
He was elected "member of parliament" for West Belfast in a British election in June 1983, a development that marked an important phase in Sinn Fein's early resurgence.

Adams headed a faction that consolidated its control of Sinn Fein in 1986 when a traditionalist old-guard faction split away, outraged at the ditching of a long-held policy of refusal to take up seats in the Dublin parliament.

He moulded a Sinn Fein power base in what he calls the "occupied territory" of Northern Ireland, which Britain rules with the support of the majority Protestant community. Sinn Fein won a raft of municipal council seats and vied with the moderate Social Democratic and Labour Party (SDLP) for Catholic support.
Adams, who has survived Loyalist assassination bids, retained West Belfast in 1987 but lost it to the SDLP in 1992.

Discussions with SDLP leader John Hume laid the basis for dramatic progress in strife-riven Northern Ireland, culminating in a London-Dublin agreement on a key policy document in late 1993 and an IRA truce of September 1994.
Adams was hailed as the man who would lead the so-called "Republican Movement" along a path of democracy. He was welcomed at the White House in Washingon by President Bill Clinton.
But optimism soured when Britain ruled Sinn Fein could not enter talks until the IRA handed over guns. The IRA said that was never part of the deal and the peace process hit quicksand.
In February 1996, the IRA ended the truce with a series of bombs on the British mainland.
Adams said a surge in Sinn Fein votes last May should have entitled him to a talks seat. The British and Irish governments insist the IRA ends violence before they will open the door to Sinn Fein.
